source.title: Implicit Regularization of Random Feature Models
source.authors: Arthur Jacot; Berfin Şimşek; Francesco Spadaro; Clément Hongler; Franck Gabriel

record.file_problem: None; the full paper and supplementary material are present.
record.tranche_reason: It varies the number of random features and measures test error around the interpolation threshold, directly testing a double-descent curve in a random-feature model.
record.gate_note: The paper also cites double-descent results from other studies; those cited results are not recorded as rows. Effective-ridge and effective-dimension calculations are not rows because they do not measure the peak location against a single complexity measure.
record.test_reason: The study sweeps the number of Gaussian random features (γ = P/N) on MNIST and reports a test-error spike at γ = 1 in the ridgeless case. It then gives a random-matrix account tying that peak to variance and to the explosion of ∂λλ̃. This bears on V4 for a non-deep model class and on the variance and ridge parts of V6. It is not one of the original sources.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that finite RF sampling equals KRR with a larger effective ridge λ̃, and that in the ridgeless limit the variance explodes at γ = 1. They prove a variance lower bound offered as a plausible explanation of double descent.
record.recipe_differences: Sweeps feature count and measures test error, as in a model-size double-descent experiment, but studies Gaussian random features (and supplementary Fourier features) rather than deep networks; the analysis fixes the training data and focuses on the feature-to-data ratio.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that adding ridge suppresses the variance explosion near γ = 1. In the N = 100 versus N = 1000 comparison, the larger sample has lower test error and a narrower cusp.

fits_no_version.finding: Finite random-feature sampling acts as an implicit ridge: the average λ-RF predictor matches λ̃-KRR, with λ̃ > λ decreasing in P.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Random-feature models with finitely many features behave like kernel ridge regression with a larger effective ridge that shrinks as features grow.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning, Proceedings of the 37th International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 119 (2020)
record.problems: The double-descent curves are shown in figures without exact numerical values or uncertainty estimates. The evidence concerns random-feature models and a limited set of MNIST and sinusoidal experiments; the data-size comparison covers only N = 100 and N = 1000.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-relevant reported results were left out. Effective-ridge curves and effective-dimension calculations were omitted because they do not test peak location against a single complexity measure.

untested.parts: No deep networks; random-feature models only.
No fixed-model-size sweep over the number of samples; the N comparison is at fixed γ = P/N.
Only Gaussian random features (and Fourier features without a reported curve shape); no other model classes; classical U-shape not examined.
Effective dimension N(λ̃) is discussed, but it is not used to predict peak location across axes.
No label-noise manipulation, no multiple peaks, no optimally tuned regularization.
No re-plotting against an effective parameter count.

missing.what: ∂λλ̃ explodes at (γ = 1, λ → 0) and stays bounded with ridge; this is the paper's mechanistic quantity behind the peak.
Sinusoidal toy data (N = 4): RF variance explodes at P = N without ridge and is suppressed by ridge.

record.verdict_notes: Mostly a theory paper; the double-descent evidence is figure-only, with no numbers or uncertainty. The V3 'challenges' label was removed because of the γ-axis confound. The V6 support rests on variance rather than test error, and the ridge value used is unstated.

versions.untested_parts: The experiments use random-feature models, not deep networks.
No sweep over training epochs or training time.
The comparison is between N = 100 and N = 1000 on MNIST, with the feature-to-data ratio swept; it does not test other sample sizes or report an increase in error from adding data.
Tests random-feature models (including Fourier features in supplementary experiments), not the full range of model classes in the claim.
The paper discusses effective dimension but does not test whether one effective-complexity measure predicts peak locations across axes.
Tests variance behavior near the interpolation threshold and the effect of ridge regularization. It does not test label-noise dependence, multiple or triple peaks, or optimally tuned regularization.
No comparison of the descent curve against an effective parameter count to determine whether it becomes an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.value: figure only; ridge curve shown alongside the ridgeless curve
rows.note: The paper states that adding ridge suppresses the variance explosion; the test-error comparison itself is shown in the figure.
rows.check: Only the Fig. 3a caption names the ridge test-error curve. The text never says whether the test-error peak is reduced or removed (it states this only for variance), and the ridge value is not given. The 'partial' state cannot be read from the text.

conditions.value: ridgeless and ridge conditions; exact ridge value not stated for this plot

rows.value: figure only; the text states that variance explodes at γ = 1 without ridge and that ridge suppresses the explosion
rows.note: The paper uses a lower bound on variance to motivate the test-error increase near the interpolation threshold.
rows.check: State is fine for the variance-driven part of V6. The row mixes two conditions: ridgeless (variance explodes at γ = 1) and ridge (explosion suppressed). Consider splitting it.

rows.subject: λ-RF predictor
rows.size_stated: P features; swept as γ = P/N
rows.operation_detail: Compare test-error curves for two training-set sizes while sweeping the feature-to-data ratio.
rows.value: N = 1000 curve; the text says test error is naturally lower and the cusp at γ = 1 is narrower
rows.note: For the sample-size comparison reported, the larger training set has lower test error rather than higher test error.
rows.check: The x-axis is γ = P/N, so comparing N = 100 with N = 1000 at fixed γ also scales P. This cannot show whether adding samples at a fixed model size raises error near the threshold, which is what V3 names. The 'reversed' state and the V3 link are unjustified.
